newsitem.title: USA: US stock analyst sees Dow 30 at 10,980 by end-97.
newsitem.headline: US stock analyst sees Dow 30 at 10,980 by end-97.

text.p: A high level of investor bearishness and a solid technical picture will drive the U.S. stock market sharply higher through the end of the year, two market analysts told the options industry conference here Saturday.
Don Wolanchuk, publisher of the Wolanchuk Report, said his year-end target for the Dow industrial average, using Elliott Wave analysis, is 10,980.
Bernard Schaeffer, president of Investment Research Institute, said his analysis of equity put-call option ratios suggests a level of 8,400 for the bellwether Dow in six months.
The Dow finished 95 points higher Friday to close at 7,071, 14 points below its record closing high of 7,085 set on March 11.

Wolanchuk said investor sentiment is at market bottom levels and that on an Elliott Wave technical basis, the Dow is near the "epicenter" of a wave three uptrend that will drive share prices sharply higher.

"The epicenter of the third wave is going to look like the crash of 1987 only upside down," he said, adding that its magnitude could be three times greater because the divisor used to calculate the Dow industrials is a third of what it was in 1987.

Using a 10-day moving average of the equity put-call ratio, Schaeffer said pessimism, as measured by high levels of put option volume compared with call volume, is reaching levels seen at other major market bottoms in July 1996, October 1992 and January 1991.
On April 24, the indicator posted a reading of 0.595, higher than the peaks in July 1996 and October 1992.
"When we have high levels of fear on pullbacks within a bull trend, that is extremely bullish for the continuation of that trend," he said.

Lawrence McMillan, head of McMillan Analysis Corp, said his analysis of equity put-call ratios flashed a buy signal recently although his momentum indicator is close to short term overbought territory.
"We'll probably get a short term sell signal in the next week or so," he said.
But he added that from a longer term perspective, the stock market is likely to be supported by a strong bond market.
He said put-call ratios for U.S. Treasury bond futures options were also high, suggesting high levels of investor bearishness.
"They're near a buy signal," he said.
One indicator that could become worrisome is the volatility in the S&P 100 stock index .OEX, he added.
The Chicago Board Options Exchange's volatility index has been holding steadily above the 20 level and has been on an upward track since early 1996.
McMillan called some of the increased volatility "random noise-type" volatility as institutional investors use the OEX more and more for arbitrage.
Even so, "overall, with volatility at these levels, it's probably not real healthy for the market longer term," he said.
Paul Ruddleston, a global technical strategist at Morgan Stanley & Co, agreed that the market had a strong upward trend, and repeated the Wall Street adage that "the trend is your friend."
But he cautioned that investors need to keep their eyes open for cracks in the market, which could begin in a market such as the dollar/mark.
